newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Germans jailed in Colombian kidnap case.
newsitem.headline: Germans jailed in Colombian kidnap case.

text.p: There were confusing accounts on Monday as to whether two German nationals -- arrested over the weekend while trying to smuggle a kidnap victim out of the country -- were themselves victims or villians of Colombia's booming kidnap trade.

The two, apparently husband and wife, were seized at the Rionegro airport outside the northwest city of Medellin at about 1 a.m. (0600 GMT) on Sunday as they tried to bundle a third German, Brigitte Schoene, aboard a charter flight to Venezuela.

Schoene, wife of a former BASF Chemicals executive, had been held since Aug. 15 by leftist National Liberation Army (ELN) guerrillas who abducted her at her Rionegro home demanding up to $6 million for her release.

Gen. Alfredo Salgado, head of the anti-kidnapping police in Antioquia, the northwest province of which Medellin is the capital, told reporters on Sunday that the two Germans arrested trying to smuggle Schoene out of the country were believed to be international financial heads and advisers of the ELN.

But Salgado offered no proof to support his allegation and other officials said the couple may have been simple intermediaries who arranged for Schoene's release in exchange for a ransom payment to the ELN.
"For all we know they were working for the poor woman's husband," one Bogota-based diplomat said.
The German embassy in Bogota has declined to comment on the arrests.

The only formal charges filed against the Germans so far stems from the fact that both were found to be carrying false identity papers. Police said names found on the papers identified the man as Norbert Schroeder, or Munich, or Jurgen Seidel. The woman's papers gave her name, alternately, as Silvia Schroeder and Isabel Seidel.

In an interview with the Caracol radio network early on Monday, Antioquia Gov. Alvaro Uribe said people who serve as go-betweens to win the release of hostages held by guerrillas were no better than guerrillas themselves.
"Intermediaries and guerrillas are the same thing in these cases," Uribe said.

A law prohibiting the payment of ransom for kidnap victims was struck down by Colombia's Supreme Court several years ago, and apart from carrying fraudulent passports Uribe did not spell out what charges the German couple could be held on.
Schoene could not be reached for comment. But Uribe quoted her as saying she had never before met the Germans who intervened to end her kidnap ordeal.
Uribe also quoted Schoene as saying she had been submitted to psychological torture during her kidnapping. "The only thing they didn't do to me was pluck my eyes out," she reportedly told Uribe.

Colombia has the world's highest kidnapping rate, with an average of about one person abducted every 2-1/2 hours. About half the kidnappings are attributed by security experts to rebels seeking to raise money for their long-running war against the state.
The ELN, Colombia's second largest guerrilla group, was founded by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966. It specializes in kidnappings and a nationwide campaign of economic sabotage.
